senses.gloss:
Ellora
------------------------------------------
Ellora—known earlier as Eḷūra has carved for itself a permanent and enviable place in the archaeological map of India because of its magnificent temple of Kailāsanātha (Śiva). It is situated on the bank of a small tributary of the गोदावरी river in Maharashtra, at a distance of 64 kms. (40 miles) from अजन्ता and 25 kms. (16 miles) from Aurangabad. There are 34 caves in all, containing Hindu, (17 caves), Buddhist (12 caves) and Jain (5 caves) constructions of various types like relief figures of mythological gods, चैत्य halls of prayer, living rooms for the bhikṣus and so on.
It is the Kailāsanātha temple built by the Rāṣṭrakūṭa king, कृष्ण I (A. D. 756-775) that is the chief attraction of एल्लोर. It is a marvellous work of art, architecture and building construction. The credit goes to the stone-cutters and carvers. There is reason to believe that they first dug a deep three-sided trench from above the hill to obtain a massive isolated block of rock 60 metres (197 ft.) long, 30 metres (98 ft.) wide and 30 metres high. The temple was then fashioned from this rocky mass, working from the top and the front, cutting away the rock, both externally and internally.
There are four parts in the temple: The main shrine, the entrance gate to the West, a separate shrine for नन्दि (Śiva’s mount) and the cloisters surrounding the courtyard.
The temple stands on a lofty plinth 7.6 metres (25 ft.) high. The friezes contain the figures of elephants and lions giving the impression that they are carrying the whole temple on their backs. The विमान (tower) over the sanctum containing the लिङ्ग, is 28.9 metres (96 ft.) in height and is three-tiered. It is in the Pallava style of temple architecture.
There is a hall (nṛttamaṇḍapa) of 16 pillars in front of the sanctum. Next to it, connected by a bridge, is an elegant shrine of नन्दि, 6 metres (20 ft.) square. On either side of this shrine there is a ध्वजस्तम्भ (flag post), 15.5 metres (50 ft.) high.
There is an imposing gateway at the front.
Around the base of the विमान, there are five miniature shrines which are now empty. They were probably meant for the सप्तमातृकास्, गणेश, Caṇḍa, भैरव and पार्वती.
Coming to the caves:
The 14th cave contains sculptures of शिव in the dancing pose of Tāṇḍava, रावण, caught under the mount कैलास, लक्ष्मी, भवानी, विष्णु and लक्ष्मी in वैकुण्ठ, as also नारायण lying on serpent शेष.
The 16th cave, measuring 83 metres (276 ft.) by 46 metres (154 ft.) is one of the finest चवे तेम्प्लेस् of India, containing a large number of sculptures depicting several incidents from the पुराणस् dealing with शिव and पार्वती.
The 17th cave, which measures 20 metres by 11 metres (64 ft. by 37 ft.) is again devoted to शिव sculptures which include images and figures of वैष्णवी, अन्नपूर्णा, पार्वती, लक्ष्मी and सरस्वती.
The Buddhist caves, are mostly plain, without any ornamentation. The 3rd and the 4th caves contain sculptures of बुद्ध seated on a lotus-throne or preaching sermons. The 12th cave contains an image of बुद्ध 3.5 metres (11½ ft.) high with other figures.
The 33rd cave is a Jaina shrine called Indrasabhā. Other caves contain the figures of Tīrthaṅkaras, Gomma-ṭeśvara (32nd cave) Yakṣas and Yakṣis.
Paintings of the अजन्ता type—but inferior in quality—have been discovered in cave no. 15 and have been assigned to the period 8th century A. D. The most striking painting is that of विष्णु and लक्ष्मी riding on the गरुड and passing through the clouds in the sky.
